html:
The Pomeranian culture was an Iron Age culture of the southern Baltic coast, in what is now northern Poland, from about 650 BCE. It is also called the Face Urn culture, after its best-known finds.

It grew out of the Lusatian culture between the lower Vistula and Parsęta rivers, then spread south until it covered most of today's Poland. Its people burned their dead and buried the ashes in graves lined with stone slabs. Some urns have a human face modelled on the side, with eyes, nose and ears, sometimes with earrings, and a lid shaped like a cap. Scenes scratched on a few urns show riders, carts and hunts.

The area lay on the Amber Road, which carried Baltic amber south toward the Mediterranean, and goods from Italy and the Celtic world came north in return. In central Poland it is closely tied to the bell-shaped burials culture, which many archaeologists see as a variant of it.

Between about 200 and 150 BCE it was replaced by the Oksywie culture in eastern Pomerania and the Przeworsk culture further south. The map keeps the label until 100 CE.
